title: An account, a repository, and getting your work off this machine
objective: By the end of this lesson you have a GitHub account, a repository you own, and a commit of yours living on a server rather than only on your laptop.

blocks.text: The git course teaches version control on your own machine for most of its length, and then asks you to push to a hosting platform. This lesson gets that account and that first push out of the way now, because creating an account and authenticating is a different kind of problem from learning git, and mixing the two is where people stall.

blocks.title: GitHub is one choice, and the courses say so
blocks.text: Git is the tool; GitHub is one company that hosts git repositories. GitLab, Codeberg and a plain server you own all work the same way for everything git itself does. The one place it matters is the continuous-integration lesson, whose YAML file is GitHub Actions specific — that lesson now says so explicitly. Use GitHub here if you have no reason to prefer another.
Authenticating: pick one and stop thinking about it

rows: HTTPS with a personal access token
Generate a token in your account settings, then use it in place of a password
The token is a password: if it leaks, it works from anywhere until you revoke it
Generate a key pair, upload the public half
One more concept now, and nothing to type later. This is what the Linux course's ssh lesson teaches

blocks.title: The public half is public; the other file never leaves your machine
blocks.text: ssh-keygen writes two files: id_ed25519.pub, which you paste into websites, and id_ed25519 with no extension, which you never send anywhere. Pasting the wrong one into a website hands over the ability to act as you. The Linux course's ssh lesson explains why the pair works; here, just get the halves the right way round.

blocks.title: Get a commit off your machine
steps: Create the account, then set up either a token or an SSH key
Verify authentication before doing anything else: ssh -T git@github.com, or push once with the token
Create an empty repository on GitHub, with no README
Follow the block above until git push succeeds
Reload the repository page in your browser and confirm README.md is there
Now prove it is really off your machine: delete the local directory with rm -rf ~/coursework/first-repo, then git clone it back
Open the cloned README.md and confirm it is the file you wrote
blocks.expected: A file you wrote, deleted from your own disk, and got back from a server. That last pair of steps is the whole point of the lesson: until you have deleted the local copy and recovered it, you have not actually established that the work is somewhere else.

cheatsheet: Git is the tool; GitHub is one host among several
Only the CI lesson is GitHub-specific, and it says so
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 makes a key pair
id_ed25519.pub is the half you paste into websites; the other never leaves your machine
ssh -T git@github.com printing your name IS success, despite the "no shell access" wording
Create the remote repository WITHOUT a README so the first push is not a merge
git remote add origin <url> then git push -u origin main
Prove it worked by deleting the local copy and cloning it back

checkpoint.prompt: ssh -T git@github.com replies "Hi yourname! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access." What happened?

choices.A: The key was uploaded to the wrong account
choices.C: Authentication failed because shell access was denied
choices.D: You need to use HTTPS instead

checkpoint.explanation: GitHub only speaks git and never gives a login shell, so that wording is expected The part that matters is your name appearing. Reading the second half as a failure is a very common false alarm.

checkpoint.prompt: ssh-keygen wrote id_ed25519 and id_ed25519.pub. Which do you paste into GitHub, and why does it matter?

choices.A: id_ed25519.pub — the other file is the private half, and handing it over gives away the ability to act as you
choices.C: id_ed25519, because it is the key

checkpoint.explanation: The .pub half is meant to be public. The file with no extension never leaves your machine.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does this lesson tell you to create the GitHub repository WITHOUT a README?

choices.D: Because git init already creates one

checkpoint.explanation: Otherwise both sides have commits and the first push is rejected as unrelated histories, before you know what that means It turns a first-push exercise into a merge problem, which is a bad place to meet your first conflict.

checkpoint.prompt: You pushed and the file appears on the website. Why does the lesson still ask you to delete the local directory and clone it back?

choices.A: Because seeing a file on a page is not proof you can get it back

checkpoint.explanation: Recovering it is The point of pushing is that the work survives the loss of your machine. Deleting and cloning is the smallest experiment that actually tests that claim.
